## BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS

Vaginitis usually presents with discharge, itching, irritation, odor, or pain.
Bacterial vaginosis is the most common form of vaginitis. Normal hydrogen peroxide and lactic acid producing vaginal flora, including Lactobacillus species, is reduced and high concentrations of anaerobic bacterial pathogens are present. Pathogenic bacteria commonly include Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma hominis, Nobiluncus, Prevotella and other Gram-negative anaerobes.
Vaginal pH should be measured, and the specimen should be examined under the microscope for identification of clue cells (epithelial cell coated with bacteria). In bacterial vaginosis the vaginal pH is high (> 4.5), the discharge is homogenous and gray-white, and the specimen has a positive amine or whiff test characterized by a fishy odor before or after addition of 10% KOH.
Bacterial vaginosis nucleic acid amplification tests are available for common pathogens to aide in identification of pathogen(s).
Bacterial vaginosis may be transmitted sexually. Patients at risk of sexually transmitted infections should be assessed for treatment.

Therapy:
## Inpatient

Preferred:
Metronidazole 500 mg PO q12h ($) [DI] for 7 days
< OR >
Metronidazole vaginal gel 0.75%, contents of 1 applicator intravaginally qhs ($)
[DI] for 5 days
< OR >
Clindamycin phosphate vaginal cream 2%, contents of 1 applicator intravaginally qhs ($) [H,O] for 7 days
Alternative:
Clindamycin 300 mg PO q12h ($) [H,O] for 7 days
